λέγει μοι ὁ ποιμήν· Μὴ θαύμαζε εἰ τὸ δένδρον ὑγιὲς ἔμεινε τοσούτων κλάδων κοπέντων. ἄφες δὲ ἕως πάντα ἴδῃς, καὶ δηλωθήσεταί σοι τὸ τί ἐστιν. 5. ὁ ἄγγελος ὁ ἐπιδεδωκὼς τῷ λαῷ τὰς ῥάβδους πάλιν ἀπῄτει ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν· καὶ καθὼς ἔλαβον, οὕτω καὶ ἐκαλοῦντο πρὸς αὐτόν, καὶ εἷς ἕκαστος αὐτῶν ἀπεδίδου τὰς ῥάβδους. ἐλάμβανε δὲ ὁ ἄγγελος τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ κατενόει αὐτάς. 6. παρά τινων ἐλάμβανε τὰς ῥάβδους ξηρὰς καὶ βεβρωμένας ὡς ὑπὸ σητός· ἐκέλευσεν ὁ ἄγγελος τοὺς τὰς τοιαύτας ῥάβδους ἐπιδεδωκότας χωρὶς ἵστασθαι. 7. ἕτεροι δὲ ἐπεδίδοσαν ξηράς, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἦσαν βεβρωμέναι ὑπὸ σητός· καὶ τούτους ἐκέλευσε χωρὶς ἵστασθαι. 8. ἕτεροι δὲ ἐπεδίδουν ἡμιξήρους· καὶ οὗτοι χωρὶς ἵσταντο. 9. ἕτεροι δὲ ἐπεδίδουν τὰς ῥάβδους αὐτῶν ἡμιξήρους καὶ σχισμὰς ἐχούσας· καὶ οὗτοι χωρὶς ἵσταντο. 10. ἕτεροι δὲ ἐπεδίδουν τὰς ῥάβδους αὐτῶν χλωρὰς καὶ σχισμὰς ἐχούσας· καὶ οὗτοι χωρὶς ἵσταντο. 11. ἕτεροι δὲ ἐπεδίδουν τὰς ῥάβδους τὸ ἥμισυ ξηρὸν καὶ τὸ ἥμισυ χλωρόν· καὶ οὗτοι χωρὶς ἵσταντο. 12. ἕτεροι δὲ προσέφερον τὰς ῥάβδους αὐτῶν τὰ δύο μέρη τῆς ῥάβδου χλωρά, τὸ δὲ τρίτον ξηρόν· καὶ οὗτοι χωρὶς ἵσταντο. 13. ἕτεροι δὲ ἐπεδίδουν τὰ δύο μέρη ξηρά, τὸ δὲ τρίτον χλωρόν· καὶ οὗτοι χωρὶς ἵσταντο. 14. ἕτεροι δὲ ἐπεδίδουν τὰς ῥάβδους αὐτῶν παρὰ μικρὸν ὅλας χλωράς, ἐλάχιστον δὲ τῶν ῥάβδων αὐτῶν ξηρὸν ἦν, αὐτὸ τὸ ἄκρον· σχισμὰς δὲ εἶχον ἐν αὐταῖς· καὶ οὗτοι χωρὶς ἵσταντο.

translation.text:
…with their whole heart[1]. So then, do you suppose that the sins of those who are repenting[b] are immediately forgiven? Not entirely. Rather, the one who repents must afflict his own soul and be humble-minded in all his conduct, resolutely, and be distressed in all kinds of tribulations; and if he bears the tribulations that come upon him, the One who created all things and strengthened them will surely be moved with compassion and will grant some healing. And this, when [God] sees the heart of the one repenting clean from everything.

And an angel of the Lord—exceedingly glorious and very tall—was standing beside the willow, holding a great sickle, and he was cutting off branches from the willow and handing them to the people who were being sheltered by the willow; and he kept giving them little rods, about a cubit long.

After all had received the rods, the angel laid aside the sickle, and that tree was sound, just as I had seen it before. I marveled within myself, saying, How is the tree sound, with so many branches cut off? The shepherd says to me, Do not marvel that the tree remained sound though so many branches were cut off[2]. But wait until you see everything, and it will be shown to you what it is.

The angel who had given the rods to the people again demanded them back from them; and in the order they had received them, so too they were called to him, and each one returned the rods. The angel of the Lord took them and examined them.

From some he received the rods dry and eaten as if by a moth; the angel ordered those who had handed in such rods to stand apart. Others handed in dry rods, but they had not been eaten by a moth; these too he ordered to stand apart. Others handed in rods half-dry; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods half-dry and having splits; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods green and having splits; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods half dry and half green; and these stood apart. Others presented their rods with two parts of the rod green and the third part dry; and these stood apart. Others handed in two parts dry and the third part green; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods almost entirely green, but a very little of their rods was dry—at the very tip; and they had splits in them[a][5][4][3]; and these stood apart.

footnotes.text: The normalized Greek here has ‘when [God] sees the heart of the one repenting clean from every …’ with the object incomplete. Many editions read ‘from every evil,’ making explicit what the sense implies.
The phrase ‘angel of the Lord’ at the start of the scene is implied by context; some lines in the source are damaged. Later in the unit the figure is explicitly called ‘the angel of the Lord.’
‘Chastise’ translates a verb that can also mean ‘torment’ or ‘put to the test’ (βασανίζω). The sense here is self‑imposed discipline of the soul in repentance.
A ‘cubit’ is an ancient measure roughly the length of a forearm (about 18 inches / 45 cm).
‘As though eaten by a worm’ reflects σητός, a worm or wood‑borer that gnaws and hollows wood; ‘worm‑eaten’ is a common rendering.

Repentance and related expressions are read in this works own context; they are not restricted to feeling sorry, and no uniform Godward formula is imposed. Use repentance for moral change while preserving the works own teaching about baptism, forgiveness, conduct and the angel of repentance; do not impose a different tradition on it.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Use repentance for moral change while preserving the works own teaching about baptism, forgiveness, conduct and the angel of repentance; do not impose a different tradition on it. Contextual editorial assessment, not independent scholarly certification.

The verb can mean ‘torment’ or ‘test.’ In Hermas’s penitential context of self‑imposed discipline, ‘chastise his own soul’ communicates severity without implying sadistic torture; we note ‘torment’ as an alternative nuance.
Keeps the cognitive/moral posture of humility (‘-minded’) explicit, matching the compound’s emphasis on attitude pervading conduct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be hard‑pressed in all kinds of tribulations
lexical_decisions.rationale: Maintains the concrete ‘pressure/tribulation’ image and preserves the intensifier ‘of many kinds’ (ποικίλαις).
‘Bear up under’ renders the prefixal nuance of enduring what comes upon one; it also fits Hermas’s frequent endurance ethic.
Preserves the visceral idiom of compassion while reading smoothly in contemporary English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the One who created all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: Formal yet clear; retains the participial description anchoring God’s identity in creation.
Compact participial rendering that fits the asyndetic description of God’s actions; ‘strengthened’ preserves active agency.
Keeps the indefinite nuance (τινα) and the concrete word ‘healing’ rather than abstract ‘relief.’
Hermas’s visionary register uses angelic intermediaries; ‘angel’ is the natural choice here.
A hand‑held harvesting or pruning tool fits the scene; ‘sickle’ is idiomatic and concrete.
The common English tree name suffices; the scene’s shade imagery is preserved.
Diminutive sense (‘little rods’) keeps size contrast with the willow’s branches and suits the later inspection.
Retains the ancient measure with an ‘about’ hedge; readers can approximate ~18 inches/45 cm.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though eaten by a worm
lexical_decisions.rationale: Conveys visible decay; ‘worm‑eaten’ is an acceptable paraphrase, noted as an alternative.
Physical ‘splits’ fits rods of wood; avoids theological overtones of ‘schism.’
‘Green’ is the natural opposite of ‘dry’ for wood imagery.
‘Dry’ matches the concrete state of wood; ‘withered’ would be more botanical than carpentry‑like.

review_passes.summary: The draft is excellent and handles the OCR corruption in the source text well. I have suggested two minor adjustments in verse 5: translating ἀπῄτει as 'demanded back' rather than 'asked to receive back', and clarifying 'καθὼς ἔλαβον' as 'in the order they had received them' to avoid the English ambiguity of 'just as they had received' (which could imply they returned the rods in the same condition they received them, contradicting the narrative).
issues_found: In verse 5, 'asked to receive them back' is a slightly clunky rendering of ἀπῄτει, which means 'demanded back' or 'asked back'.

In verse 5, 'just as they had received' (καθὼς ἔλαβον) is ambiguous in English and could be misread as 'in the same condition they had received them.' The Greek refers to the sequence/order of their calling. 'in the order they had received them' clarifies this.

revisions.rationale: Adjudicator-modified: The Greek preposition ἀπὸ means 'from,' and the adjective καθαρός (clean) construed with ἀπὸ means 'clean from' or 'purified from' something, not 'clean in' a certain respect. Translating ἀπὸ παντὸς as 'from everything' accurately reflects the provided source text (which appears to be missing 'πονηροῦ ἔργου' due to an OCR skip) and preserves the separative imagery of the Greek idiom without needing bracketed insertions.

But wait until you see everything, and it will be shown to you what it is.

translation.text: From some he received the rods dry and eaten as if by a moth; the angel ordered those who had handed in such rods to stand apart. Others handed in dry rods, but they had not been eaten by a moth; these too he ordered to stand apart. Others handed in rods half-dry; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods half-dry and having splits; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods green and having splits; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods half dry and half green; and these stood apart. Others presented their rods with two parts of the rod green and the third part dry; and these stood apart. Others handed in two parts dry and the third part green; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods almost entirely green, but a very little of their rods was dry—at the very tip; and they had splits in them; and these stood apart.

base_translation.text: …with their whole heart. So then, do you suppose that the sins of those who are repenting are immediately forgiven? Not entirely. Rather, the one who repents must afflict his own soul and be humble-minded in all his conduct, resolutely, and be distressed in all kinds of tribulations; and if he bears the tribulations that come upon him, the One who created all things and strengthened them will surely be moved with compassion and will grant some healing. And this, when [God] sees the heart of the one repenting clean from everything.

translation.text: …with all their heart. So, do you think that people who repent[a] have their sins forgiven immediately? Not completely. Instead, a person who repents must humble and afflict his own soul, remain humble in everything he does, stand firm, and suffer distress through every kind of trouble. If he bears the troubles that come upon him, the One who created all things and made them strong will surely have compassion and grant him some healing—when God sees that the repentant person’s heart is clean from everything.

The recommended wording retains the clearer distributive singular while preserving both the required return and the broader correspondence.

base_translation.text: From some he received the rods dry and eaten as if by a moth; the angel ordered those who had handed in such rods to stand apart. Others handed in dry rods, but they had not been eaten by a moth; these too he ordered to stand apart. Others handed in rods half-dry; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods half-dry and having splits; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods green and having splits; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods half dry and half green; and these stood apart. Others presented their rods with two parts of the rod green and the third part dry; and these stood apart. Others handed in two parts dry and the third part green; and these stood apart. Others handed in their rods almost entirely green, but a very little of their rods was dry—at the very tip; and they had splits in them; and these stood apart.

translation.text: Some people handed in rods that were dry and looked as though moths had eaten them. The angel told these people to stand apart. He also told each of the following groups to stand apart: those whose rods were dry but not moth-eaten; half dry; half dry and split; green and split; half dry and half green; two-thirds green and one-third dry; two-thirds dry and one-third green; and almost entirely green, with only the very tip dry, but also split.

simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The rods were dry and appeared moth-eaten without asserting that moths caused the damage.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The active wording is easier to follow while preserving the comparison to moth damage.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: Others handed in ... and these stood apart
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: He also told each of the following groups to stand apart
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The angel instructed every separately listed group to stand apart.
simplification_decisions.rationale: One framing clause reduces repetition without changing the angel's order into a physical act.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: two parts ... and the third part
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The proportions of green and dry portions remain unchanged.
simplification_decisions.rationale: Modern fractions express the same proportions more directly.

risk_flags.risk: Compressing the repeated actions could make the groups seem less distinct.
risk_flags.mitigation: Each rod condition remains a separate item governed by the angel's instruction.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: Some people handed in rods that were dry and looked as though moths had eaten them. The angel told these people to stand apart. He also set apart each of the following groups: those whose rods were dry but not moth-eaten; half dry; half dry and split; green and split; half dry and half green; two-thirds green and one-third dry; two-thirds dry and one-third green; and almost entirely green, with only the very tip dry, but also split.
